opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question. I think vision-language models have brought something really exciting to the table: a lot of world knowledge and common sense that you get from internet-scale pretraining. They can tell you that a person in a high-visibility vest waving their arms is probably directing traffic, or that a ball rolling into the street might be followed by a child. That kind of semantic understanding is genuinely valuable for the long tail of driving.

But there are several capabilities that I think still need substantial work before these models can meet the bar that driving demands.

The first is spatial and geometric reasoning. Driving is fundamentally a 3D, metric problem. You need to know not just that there's a car over there, but exactly where it is, how fast it's moving, its heading, and how that will evolve over the next several seconds, to a precision of tens of centimeters. Most VLMs are trained on 2D images paired with text, and language is a fairly lossy medium for describing precise geometry. So grounding these models in accurate 3D understanding, and fusing in other sensors like lidar and radar, is an important open area.

The second is temporal reasoning and dynamics. Driving isn't a single-frame problem. You need to track agents over time, understand their intent, and predict how multiple agents will interact with each other and with you. Many current VLMs are still fairly weak at reasoning over long video sequences and at the kind of multi-agent, interactive prediction that's central to driving.

Third is latency and efficiency. These models are large, and in a car you have strict real-time constraints and a finite compute budget onboard. You need to react within fractions of a second. So there's a lot of work on distillation, on figuring out which parts of the system benefit from the large model's knowledge, and on architectures that can run fast enough to be safe.

Fourth, and maybe most important, is reliability and verifiability. In driving, it isn't enough to be right most of the time. You need extremely low failure rates, and you need to be able to characterize and validate the system's behavior. VLMs can hallucinate, they can be confidently wrong, and their failure modes can be hard to predict. So calibration, knowing when the model doesn't know, and building evaluation frameworks that give you real confidence in safety are critical.

And related to that is closed-loop behavior. A lot of how these models are evaluated is open-loop: you show them a scene and ask what should happen. But driving is closed-loop. Your actions change the world, other agents react to you, and small errors can compound. Training and evaluating models in a way that captures that, often through high-fidelity simulation, is something we spend a lot of time thinking about.

So my view is that VLMs are a very promising ingredient, especially for semantic understanding and handling rare situations, but they work best as part of a carefully designed system. You combine their broad knowledge with strong, precise perception and prediction and rigorous safety validation. The interesting research question is how to get the best of both worlds.

r001.rationale: The response says driving requires precise 3D understanding and calls for grounding models in accurate 3D understanding.

r002.rationale: It identifies temporal reasoning as a needed capability, noting that models must track agents over time and remain weak at reasoning over long video sequences.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that vision-language models are remarkably good at the things they were built for, which is describing and reasoning about the visual world in human terms, and they're still fairly far from what driving actually asks of a system. Let me try to break it down.

The first gap is 3D and spatial understanding. Driving is fundamentally a problem of geometry and dynamics. You need to know where things are in metric space, how fast they're moving, and where they'll be in a few seconds. Most VLMs are trained on 2D images and text, and their notion of space is loose. They can tell you there's a cyclist on the right, but they struggle with "the cyclist is 14 meters ahead, closing at 3 meters per second, and will occupy my lane before I reach the intersection." That precise, quantitative spatial grounding is something we've had to build on top rather than get for free.

Closely related is temporal reasoning. A lot of these models are still essentially single-frame or short-clip reasoners. Driving requires tracking the evolution of a scene over seconds, sometimes longer, maintaining object identity through occlusion, and understanding intent. A pedestrian who glanced at you two seconds ago behaves differently from one who's looking at their phone. Capturing that over long horizons, efficiently, is an open problem.

The third area is counterfactual and causal reasoning. Driving isn't about describing the scene, it's about asking "what happens if I do X?" and "what might that other agent do in response?" Language models are good at pattern completion, but the planning problem involves reasoning about rare outcomes and interactions, often ones not well represented in any training data. The long tail is where safety lives, and it's precisely where the data is thinnest.

Then there's latency and reliability. You have maybe tens of milliseconds to react. Big generative models are expensive, and you can't have a system that hallucinates a free lane. So there's a lot of work in distillation, in making the reasoning available at the right time scale, and in building verifiable guardrails around the model's output. The failure mode we worry about isn't that the model is dumb, it's that it's confidently and fluently wrong.

And finally, I'd point to calibration and knowing what you don't know. A driving system needs to recognize when it's in a situation outside its competence and act conservatively. Current VLMs don't have a great sense of their own uncertainty. That's an area where I think combining the broad world knowledge of these models with more structured, grounded representations, and with lots of simulation and targeted data, is going to be the path forward.

So I'm quite optimistic. The world knowledge and the semantic flexibility these models bring are genuinely useful, especially for the long tail of unusual scenes, construction zones, unusual signage, emergency vehicles, things that a purely perception-trained system has never seen. But we're still in the phase of figuring out how to combine that with the precision, the temporal depth, and the safety guarantees that driving demands.

r001.rationale: It identifies 3D and spatial understanding, including precise metric positions and motion, as a gap for driving.

r002.rationale: It says driving requires tracking scene evolution over seconds or longer and identifies long-horizon temporal reasoning as an open problem.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few areas where we still need substantial progress. One is spatial understanding. A model can describe what’s in an image quite well, but for driving you need to understand precisely where things are, how they’re moving, and how those relationships are changing over time.

That temporal understanding is another big piece. You need to reason over a sequence of observations and anticipate what might happen next. Is that pedestrian about to cross? Is that vehicle starting to merge? Describing the scene is useful, but predicting how it could evolve is critical for deciding what to do.

And then there’s reliability. You need the model to handle unusual situations and recognize when it doesn’t have enough information. If something is occluded or ambiguous, that uncertainty needs to translate into appropriate driving behavior. So I see a lot of promise in the broad understanding these models bring, but connecting that understanding to precise, consistent, real-time decisions is where there’s still significant work to do.

r001.rationale: The response calls for spatial understanding and precise object locations, but does not clearly identify understanding the world in 3D.

r002.rationale: It calls for reasoning over sequences and predicting what happens next, but does not specify reasoning over several seconds or more of scene history.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the key challenges is grounding these models in the physical world. Being able to describe a driving scene is useful, but we need to understand where things are, how they’re moving, and how that situation might evolve over time. That requires a much richer understanding of geometry and motion than you can demonstrate with a caption of a single image.

There’s also the question of reasoning about interactions. If a pedestrian is standing near the curb, are they about to cross? What information would help resolve that uncertainty, and how should the vehicle behave while it’s uncertain? We need models that connect understanding to predictions and ultimately to actions.

And then reliability is critical. A model can be very impressive on a broad range of examples and still make mistakes that matter tremendously in driving. So we need better ways to evaluate these capabilities, understand the failure modes, and establish that improvements translate into safer behavior.

r001.rationale: The response mentions geometry and locating objects, but does not clearly identify understanding the world in 3D.

r002.rationale: The response mentions motion and how a situation may evolve over time, but does not specify reasoning over several seconds or more of scene history.
